utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Madam Usher, may I ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise one effectively housekeeping matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution and the Defence had agreed that the Prosecution would prepare and tender to the Court a simple list of voice identifications of intercepts covered during the course of the witness's two interviews. I have that. I see it has at least one typographical error I'd like to correct, and also I'd like to give Mr. Stewart and Ms. Cmeric a chance to see the document, but it will then be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You first show it to the Defence and then we'll hear whether there's any objection or not and give a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic. Good morning, Mr. Tomic. Please be seated. Mr. Mandic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony on the 23rd of November. Yes. Examination-in-chief has been concluded. Mr. Stewart, we discussed it already slightly yesterday. The Chamber offers the Defence the opportunity to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, as foreshadowed yesterday, the Defence's position is that we -- I think it's best to put it this way: We decline, and he hope that's not understood as impolite. We decline to cross-examine at the moment, Your Honour, while not in any sense intending to waive cross-examination. We accept on the Defence side that an application to have Mr. Mandic brought back for full cross-examination at some future date is an application which will have to be made and considered on its merits at the time it is made. And that is our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. You also understand that the Chamber will then give a decision whether or not an opportunity will be given to the Defence. If so, the Chamber will also then decide by what mode, whether that would be calling the witness back to The Hague or do it through a videolink or, well, whatever. Everything is undecided in respect of such a future application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're also aware that the previous decision on this issue limited the further cross-examination on those subjects that were contained in recently disclosed material. Of course, this could not prevent you from making a wider application, an application to fully cross-examine the witness, also on matters that were contained in earlier disclosed material. So that is the decision until now, and we'll wait and see what your application will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, Mr. Stewart, one clarification, or perhaps I should perhaps address Mr. Krajisnik directly, although I -- from the earlier messages, I may have an expectation, the Chamber may have an expectation on what the answer would be. But in the beginning of the testimony of Mr. Mandic, Mr. Krajisnik said that he would like to be in a position to put questions by himself directly to Mr. Mandic. Does it mean that that request is moot now as well, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps. I -- may we, I suggest, deal with it this way: I anticipate that there is no point in my making any submission in relation to that matter myself this morning, as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel, and if I invite Your Honour perhaps respectfully to address that request to Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not in any sense endorsing or welcoming or inviting that request. It just is -- it's moot in the way that Your Honours suggests that I should waste any time saying anything about it. But I do suggest that at least Your Honour might simply put that request to Mr. Krajisnik for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the Court proceeds, if I may just make the Prosecution's position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And therefore all of the issues present here. I don't think it comes as any surprise to the Defence or the Court that the Prosecution's position is that an order was made and that the declination to proceed with cross-examination at this time is in fact a waiver of cross-examination, and therefore, once the Court has proceeded with its questions, if it has any, this witness's testimony is concluded. Now, obviously that doesn't preclude the Defence from filing whatever submissions it may have in the future, but I think it needs to be made clear that that's the case. Insofar as documents that may have been the subject of -- that were the subject of the Court's order before are concerned, there would have been a variety of ways of dealing with those, including examining them individually to see what kind of impact they might or might not have had on the cross-examination, and having appropriate responses to whatever that situation was. So I don't think there's any -- in the event that the Prosecution -- that the Defence files a later motion, there's certainly no fixed position, we submit, with respect to those documents, and again, if and when such submission was made by the Defence, they would have to be examined on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The position of the Prosecution is clear. Mr. Krajisnik, you raised the issue of whether you could put questions to this witness directly. As you've heard, Mr. Stewart invited me to, since it was a personal request by yourself, to ask you whether that request still stands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, thank you, Your Honours, for giving me this opportunity to address the Trial Chamber once more. I did ask you to put some questions to this witness here, and I uphold my request. I think that would be very useful, because of what I've already said, and I want to repeat it in front of the witness here. The witness interprets certain things in a certain manner simply because he has forgotten certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- in front of the witness whatever is being said. The witness should leave court straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there's another matter, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, you may express whether you still wish to put questions to this witness. You're not allowed to comment on the testimony given by this witness at this moment. That's not something -- and if you think that there's any specific reason to do that, then it should be done in the absence of the witness. But I already tell you that usually cross-examination, that is, putting questions to the witness by the opposite party, serves, among other things, the purpose to test the reliability and credibility of the witness, and it will become clear from any questions whether that purpose is sought to be achieved. But it's not appropriate to comment on the content of the testimony given by this witness. So if you insist on doing it, I think I made clear that at this moment the Chamber doesn't see any specific reason, because if it has to be -- it's clear, I would say; it's implicit in the right to cross-examine a witness that the opposite party may have different views on what the witness testified about. So, therefore, I don't think it's necessary for you to expand on it, but if you want -- if you insist on doing it, then at least the witness should leave the courtroom for a while. So, therefore, I'd like to know whether you still have the wish to put questions to the witness. And if further --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the first matter raised, I do apologise, and I fully agree with you that I should not have said those things. And there is no need for me to mention them in the presence of the witness. As for your question, I sat down with Mr. Stewart the day before yesterday, and we discussed our examination of Mr. Mandic, and both of us concluded that Mr. Stewart was not in a position to examine the witness at present. Since it is very important for me to have this witness examined by Mr. Stewart, and I possibly put some additional questions to the witness, I thought it would be highly improper for me to now examine Mr. Mandic, because my counsel is not in a position to do this at present. Because I am satisfied with the services provided by my counsel and I do want him to play his role. That's why I appeal to you, Your Honour, not to deny us the right to cross-examine Mr. Mandic. I told you my reasons for it. I told them to you in a closed session. And I think it would be highly useful for all of us here, including Mr. Mandic, to clear up the truth at this trial. That's why I stand by my request, and I appeal to you to approve and grant the request that will be put to you in this respect by Mr. Stewart at a later stage to cross-examine the witness, and I hope that in this manner we will all be able to establish the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. It is my duty to draw your attention to the fact that if you say I'd like to add some questions to the questions put in cross-examination at a later stage by Mr. Stewart, that whether or not you get such an opportunity, of course, depends on whether any application will be granted at a later stage to recall Mr. Mandic for cross-examination. I take it that you are aware of that, so that if you say now "I'd rather join counsel in a later cross-examination," that if there will be no later cross-examination, that then, of course, you have the possibility of putting questions to this witness has then been -- has been gone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am fully aware of that, but I have to ask -- kindly ask you the following. In addition to being Judges, you were also attorneys at law. It would really be highly improper of a client to basically sabotage his counsel, and I do agree with Mr. Stewart when he says that at this stage he's not prepared to carry out cross-examination. And I have to draw your attention to the following fact: That some of the material I received only yesterday. I spent the entire night examining the materials, because some of the things were completely new to me. That is why I thought it proper to proceed this way. And in addition, we thought that if we were to proceed now and not call Mr. Mandic at a later stage, this would leave the entire matter incomplete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your position, and you've clearly expressed that you're aware of your present procedural situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then -- Mr. Mandic, at this moment the Defence will not examine you, not cross-examine you, as you may have concluded from the discussion you just witnessed. Therefore, we proceed, and questions of the Bench will be put to you. First of all, Judge Canivell will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, please, you had told us that while you were in your position as minister of justice, you were informed, you got information about what was the situation in the locations in which people were detained. I would like to be aware of what was the extent of your knowledge. Do -- you have recognised that, I believe, people, civilians, were put in detention in those places, but what else did you know about that? Did you know about mistreatment of these persons in the places in which they were retained?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was appointed minister of justice, the civilian one, on 19th of May, my first task was to organise the civilian justice administration and to collect data as a minister, who was in some way in charge of the commissions that were collecting information on the camps held by the police and the military. However, it was very difficult to obtain the information, since Bosnia and Herzegovina's communication lines and roads were severed and cut off. It was very difficult. That is why, at the level of the entity of Republika Srpska, an organ was established, headed by Ms. Biljana Plavsic, together with the international community, to encompass all the branches of government, the executive and the legislative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for your answer, but what I wanted to know is what was the level of your knowledge of the situation in those places. You say that some of them were not easily reachable, but of course most of them would be, since they were in the power of the Bosnian Serbs community, presidents of this community. So what did you really know about what was happening there? You knew that besides being detained, these people there, they were object of mistreatment, they were beaten, they were tortured. What else did you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just mentioned the lines -- communication lines and roads that were severed. For instance, we had no communication whatsoever with Krajina, and I mean Banja Luka and the Krajina there and the Krajina in Croatia. So we -- there were no communication lines. Likewise, the situation was similar in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where we had very little information about the camps and the treatment there. Whenever we received any information, and we would most often receive them from the international community and from the Muslim side, that these were information that we received through MUP, we would process the information and act upon them, both through the government and through the ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Are you then meaning that the international information was a better one than your own information about the situation in these places, in your country?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: When you got this information, what did you do? I mean, you have to verify that. Even I realise that you tried to make -- pass the situation under the normal justice system as a minister of justice, you tried that. But before that - and besides, it wasn't successful, if I recollect well - what did you really know about what was going on in these places, after the accusations of the data that was provided by the international sources?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've said that a moment ago. We would act upon every piece of information by establishing commissions that would go on the ground, with the approval of the military, because it was usually the military that held these collection centres. But this would not take place at the level of the Ministry of Justice, which was a civilian ministry, but at the level of the state. Because that was the only possible way for us to get informed about different camps, that is prisons scattered in different parts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Well, I would like to touch another subject. You recognised yesterday that when the list of the 57 locations that were provided to you and about which Mrs. Plavsic explained what she felt necessary in the television, you recognised yesterday that some of these places were located in Serbia. But what about the others? You knew about the existence of the others? You knew about the people that were inside? Relate it with what I had asked you before.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list that I saw yesterday was actually the first time I ever saw it. I knew on that list that several places were outside the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was Biljana Plavsic who was in charge of these matters. I was aware of some of those locations that she mentioned, but these were mostly within the Sarajevo area, the canton of Sarajevo, whereas Ms. Plavsic got her information on the other places through the military, through the MUP, or through the top leadership. And the list that we saw here, yesterday or the day before yesterday, was a list that I saw for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that some facts that you were asked about were general knowledge. Did you think or had you observed that that was general knowledge among a list the leadership or even down than the higher leadership of the Serbian -- the Bosnian Serbs, that these camps existed and what was done in these camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a very small number of people from the very top leadership of Republika Srpska would know that, and that would be more the military than the civilian leadership. In Hotel Bistrica on Jahorina, that's where the government seat was, and it was difficult to have communication with territories outside the area of Sarajevo. We gained more information through CNN and other international TV stations in Sarajevo than we were able to discover through other media and local television. And there was some information that we received for the first time from the Muslim media. And for the most part, we did not trust them, because we felt that this was a sort of propaganda war going on. Yesterday I noticed that the lists that Mrs. Plavsic had before her were exaggerated by both sides with respect to the number of prisons and the number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I would ask you, then, another question. You got personally the impression during these times that the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Serb leadership had lost grasp of the situation, I feel. You didn't realise, you didn't know what was going on, not even in war, not even what was happening in the territories that were under your domination?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serbs was already divided before the war into the SAO Krajinas and these were closed and independent systems of government. They were a kind of confederation with respect to the central authorities. The SAO Krajinas had their own armies, police, governments, presidents, and all the other institutions that constituted an overall authority. That's how it was with the SAO Majevica and Semberija, that's how it was with the SAO Hercegovina, and that's how it was with the SAO, I think, of Romanija or Sarajevo. I can't remember precisely. So each of these had all the institutions of military, civilian, and police power, and all other institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: But you haven't answered exactly what I asked you. I asked you if in fact you had the impression personally that the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Serb leadership in this situation has lost grasp, has lost the possibility of knowing and directing the situation to a final that be acceptable for their purposes. Is that the case? You got the impression that you were completely at a loss in this moment and that, well, the situation was lost? I mean, what was the feelings, the feelings you appreciated and other people around you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first months of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, the state was consolidated and the central government began to function and take over control of all the territories controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. And I think that by the end of 1992, they had taken full control over all these autonomous provinces, that is, on the entire territory controlled by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: And when do you think it arrived to this situation, the situation was reached? You said at the beginning not, but when the situation was, let's say, stabilised for the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this happened in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Be more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: September or October, the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi will have one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I would like to ask you some clarifications. Do not forget that you are the witness of the Trial Chamber, now that you are in this courtroom, you are the witness of the Trial Chamber, of the Tribunal, and I would like to draw your attention on one fact. It might seem quite a minor fact at the beginning, but I would like to ask Madam Registrar to give Mr. Mandic the document which has the following exhibit number: P452. Mr. Minister, I would like to draw your attention to one fact. The names that you see on this document do not have the same spelling. When you compare the translation and the original document, you do find out that the names do not have the same spelling. So I would like you to concentrate or to focus your attention on the original document, and you might see that the first name, or that the second name has as a first name "Amira." Is that a man or a woman? Because in the English translation, we see that the name is "Amir." And I do think that Amir might be the name of a man, whilst Amira is the name of a woman, I think.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order -- this is Bosnian. This is a man. Muharemovic Zejnila and Pandzic Amira. It could be "Mensuda" or "Mensuda." It depends on where you lay the stress. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But is Mensuda the name of a man or a woman? And what about Amira? Amira and Mensuda?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Amir is a man's name.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case, it's "Amira." The nominative is "Amir." "Mensud" is the nominative. "Mensuda." So -- and then the stress would be different in the case of a male or a female name. "Mensuda" would be the nominative of a female name. Mensuda is a male name. For example, in Serbian, "Sava" and "Sava," Sava is a female name and Sava is a male name. They have the same letters, but it depends on the stress whether it's a male or a female name. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So when you take a look at this document, you realise straight away that they're talking about men or women? I'm still talking about the original document, of course. I'm talking about the original document in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it says here in the first line male prisoner "zatvorenike," which means male prisoners, not the -- if it referred to female prisoners, it would have said "zatvorenice," not "zatvorenike." "Zatvorenike," that usually refers to men. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But in the English translation, this is not so clear. In any case, it's not as clear as you're telling us. And I quote in English: [In English] "Listed below." [Interpretation] So you're telling us that this is not a problem for you, but you do understand that this document is a document about men and not about women. So you see what is written in the first line, and could you please tell us what is the precise word that is so clear for you and that means that we're talking about men --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] -- zatvorenike.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 2, had it been a woman, it would have been "Pandzic Amiru" in the accusative case, not "Amira." Under 3, it would have been "Pandzic Mensudu" not "Mensuda."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that it's a question of nominative and accusative case. There are seven cases in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, it is certainly about men. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this clarification. I would like to draw your attention on another document, and I would like to invite Madam Registrar to give you the said document. This is Exhibit number P453. This document has been signed by someone else, but you do see that your name appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So in this document, the detention facility of Butmir needs some 50 war prisoners, and I'm quoting in English once more: Necessary to send 50 war prisoners who are in good health to penal and correctional facility Butmir."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I would like to put to you a question, sir. The prisoners of war were supposed to do some kind of work. Was it a compulsory type of work? In other words, were they forced? Were they obliged to do this type of work? As far as you know, of course. Were they paid for this type of work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I will tell you why this is not my signature. This is not my signature because it doesn't look like my signature. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to interrupt you, sir. This was not my question. I don't want to know who signed instead of you, without indicating that this was not your signature. This was not the main purpose of my question. My question is quite different, in fact. I would like to know whether you are able to tell me whether the prisoners of war, which are needed in this detention facility in order to do some work, I would like to ask you whether this work was compulsory for the prisoners of war, or I would like to know whether the prisoners of war could refuse to do the work. Were they paid for the work that they were doing? This is just a very simple question that I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they could have refused to do the job if they were required to do so by the authorities, and they were not paid for their work. If you will allow me, Your Honour, to expand on this. The Koka farm, which before the war belonged to the penal and correctional facility Butmir, was a source of food, not only for the prisoners but also for the persons in Kula. And probably the people who were administering the prison were looking for workers to work on the Koka farm. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But as far as you're aware, was it only there that this job -- that they were supposed to do this type of job, or was it quite normal that prisoners of war had to do some type of work, some type of jobs? And what type of jobs are we talking about? Are you able to give us this type of information about the work that they were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Butmir penal and correctional facility or to prisons in general? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No. I'm talking about detention facilities where prisoners of war were detained. I would like to know whether the prisoners of war were forced to do some jobs, and if that is the case, what type of work were they supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not inside the prisons, but for the needs of the army and the police, the army and the police had the right to require certain numbers of prisoners to take them and have them dig trenches or do similar types of work in order to defend certain features and facilities. So they were able to request prisoners. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And this was quite common; this was a type of common information. I guess that everyone within the government knew or was aware of this type of information. How did you find out about this detail?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was governed by the law on the military, on the army. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] The law on the military, on the army, in other words, the army requested prisoners of war to do some type of compulsory jobs, and you were talking about digging up trenches, for instance. They had to do this type of work, then, and this is governed by the military code? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And is that also true of the police? Because you've just told us that the prisoners of war could be requested by the army or by the police.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case of an imminent threat of war, in case of an imminent threat of war, and that was the situation, the army was superior to the police. The police were subordinate to the army and had to behave in compliance with the law on defence. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And was an order or a decision taken in order to declare the imminent threat or the fact that the war or the conflict was about to break out? Was this the case at the time? And since when? From when? When was this decision taken? Would you remember about the date, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That decision was made at the very beginning of the war, in March or April 1992. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And who took this decision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Assembly of Republika Srpska, at the initiative of the president of the Republic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You said that in such a case, the army was superior. So I would like to put a question to you. Did the army depend on someone? In other words, was the army subordinated to the civilian authority or was it working under the influence of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The supreme military commander was the president of the Republic, and the chief of the General Staff was the second-ranking man, issuing orders to the army. They were responsible to no one but their own institutions, from the lowest to the highest. The chief of the General Staff and the president of Republika Srpska. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And during the time that you yourself was the minister of justice, and if I'm not mistaken, I think that you took your office in May 1992 until the end of November of 1992. Could the cabinet of ministers control the army? Did they have a say in it? Or what was the role of the civilian cabinet of ministers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was a military justice system, and the chief of the General Staff was in charge of it. He was in charge of all segments of military power and authority. The civilian authorities, even the government, were unable to make decisions contrary to the law on defence and the positions of the army and the president of the Republic. This was the case when an imminent threat of war had been declared and when all institutions were subordinated to the military. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So if I understand you well, you're telling us that even if the army abuses its power, the civilian power had no way of intervening; they just could not intervene?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not intervene. Let me explain this. It would happen for the military to imprison certain ministers and keep them in prison for ten days. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And was that done with the agreement or the approval of the president of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was the chief of the General Staff. If he disagreed with some decisions made by certain ministers, he would keep them in prison for ten days at a time. Even the minister of the military was imprisoned in this way, and he was given the task of feeding cattle and livestock. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I would like to touch upon another subject, if you please. I would like to talk about the centre of power within the Serb Republic of Bosnia. On a number of occasions during the March 2004 interview, and here, during your testimony, you've talked about what you called the leadership of the Republika Srpska. And you told us the following: You told us that Dr. Karadzic controlled the police and the army and that this conferred him a certain power. You told us that he could build his own power, whereas Mr. Krajisnik had with him the MPs, the deputies, and the president of municipalities. This is what you told us.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, you yourself do not believe that Mr. Krajisnik had any power over the military or the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not over the army, because in the beginning, with the chief of the General Staff -- and this was in compliance with the laws, this was concerning the compliance with the laws, that they came into conflict, and they were basically in conflict since between mid-1992 until the end of the war, and in this period, they had very few contacts and he was unable to influence the situation in the war. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I did not receive interpretation for this answer. Is there a difficulty? I am addressing the interpreters now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may a few words in English, Judge El Mahdi, then perhaps you find out whether there's any interpretation. Yes, please proceed. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [In English] Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You always find a solution for everything. There was mention of the authority of Mr. Krajisnik with regard to the army. You have stated, I quote in English: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] " -- army." [Interpretation] Can I conclude from this that you drew a distinction between the army and the police, which means that he did have the possibility to exert influence over the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partly, Your Honour, over the police, but that was only in part. But not as regards the war operations and the combat operations. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But did the Territorial Defence come under the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army. That was the reserve force of the army. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Fine. You have stated that the police had also taken part in the military operations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] By doing so, the police was in a position to have prisoners of war; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In your opinion, and based on your knowledge, the events that took place within the detention facilities held by the police, that is to say, the information about what was going on in these detention facilities, were forwarded to which levels? Who was in charge of these facilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Republic, prime minister, and different ministers, ministers of defence, minister of police, until the end of 1992. Later on, the minister of justice was also the one to receive information on these issues. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to turn now to a topic that is related to what we have just been mentioning, which is the relationship between the legislative and the executive branches of government, that's to say between the government and the Assembly. I am aware of the fact that initially the difficulties lay in the fact that you were trying to establish this state, the Republic, that was in the making. I would like you to tell me now what sort of a relationship existed between the executive branch of government, that is, the government itself, and the Assembly. That was the legislative branch of government.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, and for the most part of the first half of the war, the legislative power was wielded by the president of the Republic. Under the constitution Article 83, I believe it was, he was entitled to pass laws himself, without the parliament, concerning all spheres of life: The army, police, justice, all the areas. The parliament had the duty to verify the law passed by the president of the state at its next session. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but did the government answer to the Assembly for its activity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] For instance, in this case, the government would report to the Assembly about its actions taken and activities. As far as you know -- let me just find an appropriate term for this. Can you tell us: Was the government informed about the goings-on on the ground? And I primarily refer to what was going on in the detention facilities. In other words, the destiny of the detainees, was it in some way told about it to the parliament deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MPs were very well-informed about the goings-on on the ground. They came from different areas, from different municipalities. They had firsthand information from the area where they resided in. As for the government and the level of the information that it had about the collection and detention facilities, they received information from the army and the police, and they received as much information as there was. But the main sources of information were the army and the police respectively, from the detention facilities that they held, and these were all the detention facilities that existed until the end of 1992 where prisoners were held. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But to your knowledge, were there discussions at the sessions of the Assembly concerning the treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And what conclusions were taken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such acts, if any, and there were such acts, they were definitely condemned for the fact this they were contrary to the Geneva Conventions governing prisoners. Commissions were established, people were tasked, and all efforts were taken to bring these practices within the realm of legality, to dissolve, disband these detention facilities, and this was done until, I believe, mid-1992. People were tasked, be it from the parliament or from professional services, but from all the levels of government. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. If I've understood you correctly, you were very closely related with Mr. Krajisnik in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got to know Mr. Krajisnik in early 1992, and we started cooperating while I had the capacity of a deputy minister for justice in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Mr. Krajisnik was president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Did you say in early 1991 or 1992 that you got to know Mr. Krajisnik? When was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991. We lived in Sarajevo. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. 1991. I wanted to verify this, because the year 1992 was entered into the transcript. So you were a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, the fact that you were appointed to that post was thanks to Mr. Krajisnik, as far as I've understood your testimony so far.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You were chosen by the prime minister; however, it was Mr. Krajisnik who gave his approval for that; is that not true? You said that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he supported. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] While you held this office, you were on friendly terms with him; you cooperated with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, and later on as well. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. You also stated that you were removed from this position because Ms. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic, for certain reasons, requested that you leave the position, regardless of the fact that Mr. Krajisnik had earlier given his support to you, in this case, he was unable to do anything else to keep you at your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only mentioned one of the reasons. In September 1992, as early as September 1992, at the Assembly session in Bijeljina, I asked that I be assigned the position of minister without an office and to be sent to Belgrade, to work there. So basically this decision coincided with my wishes. And when the first government was dissolved, it was solely Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic who asked that I not be included into the government of Republika Srpska in any form, because we had -- we were in a personal conflict, Ms. Biljana Plavsic and myself, since the beginning of 1992. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I will rephrase the question that I put to you. In your opinion, the ministers who formed part of the government after the resignation of the prime minister Djeric, who actually elected them into the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following prime minister, the prime minister who was to follow, was Mr. Lukic, and he was Mr. Koljevic's man of choice. He actually proposed him, and this was accepted by the political and state leadership of Republika Srpska. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Who elected them? Who appointed them? If you know. By whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Assembly that elected them, and they probably consulted with the political leadership of Republika Srpska. I think that this government was elected in January 1993. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] When you say that they were elected by the Assembly, what do you mean by that? Did Mr. Krajisnik have a say in this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was unanimous support in relation to the cabinet of Mr. Lukic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but you've said that the choice was Mr. Koljevic's, and my question is: Is this true also for members of his team? You now tell me that they were essentially elected by the Assembly, the deputies in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Koljevic suggested that Mr. Lukic be elected as prime minister and that this proposal was supported by the political structures of the state leadership of Republika Srpska. Naturally, the MPs and the political leaders were consulted also with regard to the ministers themselves. And there was unanimous support of all the structures for this government of Mr. Lukic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You say "state structures." I will quote what you said in English: [In English] "Leadership of Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] When you say this, what do you exactly mean by it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political means, the core leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, that was the party bearing the power in Republika Srpska, and the state functionaries were the ones heading the state, the parliament, and certain regions. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Can you be more precise and tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The personnel policy was run at the time by Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, Rajko Dukic, and some other leaders of the regional boards of the Serbian Democratic Party whose names I cannot recall at present. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But within this narrow circle of people, were there any conflicts taking place or were these people always unanimous and agreed on all the issues? You've mentioned here now five persons, about five names, but did they ever come into conflict with each other, or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different views and proposals, but they were discussed with a view to being streamlined. And the state leadership at the time was unanimous in its positions to a large degree. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] The last topic that I would like to discuss here is the following one: Do you recall saying, when talking about the source of power and his competence, the competence of Mr. Krajisnik, you said that on the one hand he relied on the MPs, and on the other, on the presidents of the municipalities, that he wielded his power from these two sources. Is that right? Did the presidents of the municipalities communicate with Mr. Krajisnik? In what way, if so? And when need arose, did they receive instructions or commands, orders from Mr. Krajisnik? If you have any knowledge of this, could you please help me with this.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was held in high esteem by the Serbian people and by the MPs, because he represented the continuity of the Assembly that used to be the Joint Assembly previously in Bosnia-Herzegovina. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to interrupt you, because this was not my question. I have to remind you of my question. It was a very simple one. You've said that he wielded his influence on the basis of the relationship that he had with the presidents of the municipalities. I asked you whether there was a flow of information, that's to say, directives, instructions, and orders, between Mr. Krajisnik, on the one hand, and the presidents of the municipalities, on the other. Do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as concerns the flow of information, but I know that people did come to Mr. Krajisnik to consult with him, people from different parts of Republika Srpska, presidents of municipalities and the MPs alike. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the presidents of the municipalities at present. If you have no knowledge of this, you may say so freely.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the information is concerned, I have no knowledge of it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Very well. You have mentioned paramilitary groups, formations. Among others, you mentioned the ones that were based at the Jewish cemetery, among others. You meant the Jewish cemetery in Sarajevo; is that right? Who were these paramilitary groups subordinate to? If I've understood you correctly, when talking of these paramilitaries based at the Jewish cemetery, you said that these were paramilitaries who came from outside.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These were members of the Serbian Radical Party, the president of which was Mr. Vojislav Seselj. But there were initially people from Sarajevo who were members of this party. The chief of this paramilitary group was Aleksic Slavko who lived in Sarajevo and was from Sarajevo, but he was a member of the party and he received instructions from Mr. Seselj. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But weren't these paramilitaries subordinate to someone, the army, the municipalities? In what way were they able to be there, to exist there, without receiving support from someone?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, these paramilitaries were under the system of the army, because General Ratko Mladic tried to place all the paramilitary groups under the command of the army. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, the municipalities were not in a position to control or coordinate the activities of the paramilitary formations active in their respective territories?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, Your Honour, they were. These paramilitary formations were present in addition to crisis staffs in certain municipalities, but from time to time the army would place both the paramilitary groups and the TO under their command, and they would form part of the unit. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Do you mean to say that in the beginning they were subordinate to the crisis staffs? That's one question. Second: Which period in time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the beginning of the war, March, April 1992, and I'm referring to the crisis staffs organised by the municipal governments. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, these crisis staffs controlled, in a manner of speaking, these paramilitaries active in the territorial of a given municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Minister. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we are close to the time where we usually have a break. I would have some questions for you as well, but perhaps I'll not finish in two minutes. Therefore, we'll have a break first and we'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mandic. If you'll just allow me one second. Mr. Mandic, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the relation between civilian authorities and military authorities. You told us that the army took over all responsibility for special MUP units. They were under the command of the army, you told us. Could you explain to us why they took over, who decided that they took over the command over the MUP units, whether they took over command of other units as well.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution of Republika Srpska and the law on the armed forces and the Ministry of the Interior, governed this, so these laws governed this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what, then, triggered -- I mean, you say "governed this." Under what circumstances, then, the MUP, the special MUP units were placed under the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is an imminent threat of war. This was declared in early 1992, and that is when the special purpose units and the active police force were placed under the command of the army. As for war operations and public law and order, the police acted independently when maintaining public law and order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say this was declared early 1992. Did this ever develop into a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Your Honours, no; at least, not as long as I was in the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that because, in your view, there was no war or that it was just not declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I think the decision was made by the president of the Republic that a state of war not be declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was the position of the president of the Republic of Srpska that a state of war not be declared and to prepare the army and police and maintain the situation as it was. That's all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was a positive decision not to declare a state of war, which is not the same as that there was no decision to declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The former was the case, not the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Then I'd like to ask you something about the National Security Council. Are you aware of the existence and the functioning of such a council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of the war, there was a form of - I don't know what the name was - but in March or April -- I can't recall what the title was now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it assist you if we received evidence that there was an organisation called the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Security Council. Maybe Mr. Tieger could assist me. I don't know what the name of the body was in March or April, but it met to discuss security, and I attended those meetings on occasion, several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're invited to assist Mr. Mandic in refreshing his memory. Well, I take it that you have discussed this, then, in your interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On what basis is counsel invited to refresh a witness's memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's rather unorthodox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the witness says that he has a body in his mind of which he does not know exactly the name, but from addressing Mr. Tieger, the Chamber understands that this must have been the subject of any conversations with Mr. Tieger, and therefore, Mr. Mandic invited Mr. Tieger to refresh his memory as to the name he used at that time for such a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our submission is that it's not proper for that invitation to be endorsed by the Trial Chamber, that counsel has, with respect, no business in becoming involved in the witness's evidence. If the witness can remember things himself, he can remember them; and if he can't, he can't. And it's not for counsel to start intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was Mr. Mandic who asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, Your Honour, in our submission. The witness may ask, but when the witness asks for counsel to assist him by giving him the facts, it remains improper wherever the invitation request comes from, it remains an improper function of counsel. I'm not suggesting any impropriety by Mr. Tieger. If he's invited and if the invitation is endorsed by the Trial Chamber, he would naturally do it, but we do say it's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's what I was rising to do. Would it be of any assistance to the Court to look at P433.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P433. Let me just try to find P433. Perhaps, Madam Registrar, I have to dig it up from my pile. A document shown to you as P433 is a document containing the minutes of the meeting of the Council for National Security and the government held on the 24th of April, 1992. Is that the body you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you tell us a bit more. We took a different road, Mr. Stewart, which is not an expression of the Trial Chamber that it follows your suggestion that it would be inappropriate; it's just undecided, and we followed a different route. Could you tell us about the functioning of that Council for National Security, or as it's sometimes translated, National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not privy to the functioning of that council, Your Honour, but I know that it was headed in that year by the president of the Republic to vice-presidents of the Republic, the chief of the General Staff, the prime minister, the minister of defence, the minister of the interior, and I don't know whether there was the President of the Assembly or not, but I do know that General Ratko Mladic and Dr. Biljana Plavsic asked that there should not be the President of the Assembly in the council, while others wanted that to happen. But I don't know what the final decision was. All this was published in the Official Gazette, that is, which leaders of Republika Srpska were members of the Council for National Security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know anything about the task of that Council for National Security?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, as minister of justice, had no idea on what the task of this legal body would be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw my own conclusions, and I can say that this had to do with the war and with war operations. There were rules regulating the operation of this council. But I wasn't really well informed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I would tell you that we received evidence that ex officio members of the National Security Council included the president of the Assembly and the prime minister, does this -- you would then say that you would still not know whether that's correct or ...?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is testimony to this effect, that is if it’s in the Official Gazette, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said it had -- you could think of it having to do anything with the war, but no further information ever reached you about tasks and functioning of this body?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the top leadership was in that council, and they were the ones who made decisions about all segments of authority in the Republic of Srpska. The very name of the Council for National Security tells us that these people dealt with the security of the country, and they had the highest powers and authorities in connection with the war in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were dealing with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- military matters as well. I take it, at least, that when you say in connection with the war, the highest powers, that that would include military matters.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring primarily to military matters, but also everything else that had to do with security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer to that question. You told us that you had quite some difficulties in getting information because of failing links with several areas of the Republic, and you told us that you would receive information from CNN and other media. Let me just read to you exactly your testimony in this respect. You said the following: "In Hotel Bistrica, on Jahorina, that's where the government seat was, and it was difficult to have communication with territories outside the area of Sarajevo. We gained more information through CNN and other international TV stations in Sarajevo than we were able to discover through other media and local television." What other international TV stations you had in mind when you gave this answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the headquarters at Pale, where the president of the Republic and the president of the Assembly were, and others, there were satellite dishes, and we could follow quite a number of TV channels on satellite television. We could also view the federal Sarajevo television station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although you here mention specifically Hotel Bistrica on Jahorina, what's the meaning of this location in the context of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the seat of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at least I understood your answer to be that in the seat of the government you were to receive CNN, since you specifically mentioned that. You now say in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether there was a satellite dish on Hotel Bistrica, but I am sure that where the president of the Republic, Karadzic, was and the president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, were, that they did have satellite dishes and they could view those television stations. Hotel Bistrica is on the top of Mount Jahorina. It's a mountain chalet. It was used by skiers before the Olympic games.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say we gained more information through CNN. Who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us in the government and those who were in the areas of Pale, Bistrica, eastern Sarajevo, and so on and so forth, the people who had contact with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Including yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just try to verify: In your interview, you were asked about media coverage in early August 1992. The question included the great international outcry about the existence of camps in Serbian-held territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When asked about this, part of your answer was that it was very difficult to communication with other parts in Republika Srpska. And then the next part, I'll read that out literally, is: "How was I supposed to watch CNN in Jahorina or read the English papers? The only newspapers that we would read were the ones that would arrive from Serbia." Is it a correct understanding of the testimony you just gave that the answer to the question you put at that time in your answer, "How was I supposed to watch CNN in Jahorina?", that the answer to that question was that you received CNN in Jahorina through the - how are they called? - these satellite receivers. I mean, you're almost denying - although not literally - that you could have received. You said, "How was I supposed to watch CNN?" And now you clearly tell us that you watched the international media.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Jahorina, as I've just said, that's where Hotel Bistrica was. I'm not sure there was a satellite dish there. However, at Pale and the office of the president and the president of the Assembly and others, there we could watch satellite TV and whatever was broadcast via satellite TV. But I'm not sure about Hotel Bistrica on Jahorina. I'm not sure we could watch satellite television there. I don't think we could, although now I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The sequence of questions in your interview was whether you were aware of this international outcry on the camps. Then you said: "I was not aware," because you were the minister of civilian judiciary. Then the question was put to you that the interviewer was not interested in whether you received any official reports, but he was talking about headlines, newspapers, covers of magazines worldwide, and CNN reports. And then you said: "How could I see CNN reports?" Do you agree with me that that is an evasive answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was an evasive answer, Your Honour. I was only saying what I felt to be true at the time. In Bistrica and down there in Sarajevo, I couldn't watch CNN. However, at Pale, in some offices belonging to high-ranking dignitaries, I was able to watch satellite TV; however, this was not on a regular basis, it was not continuous. CNN journalists would even arrive in Pale and interview people there. The whole of public life took place at Pale, around the president's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. My next question concerns the interview that was shown to you by the interview of Mrs. Plavsic. Ms. Plavsic was giving comment on a list of detention facilities, and she said that the 3.000 persons detained in Omarska were there on the basis of a judicial decision. You commented on this interview by saying that from both sides war propaganda was given. As far as the 3.000 Omarska prisoners are concerned, and specifically the explanation by Mrs. Plavsic that they were there on the basis of a judicial order, do you consider this to be war propaganda or to be the truth?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible that the judiciary could have brought such a large number of people to Omarska through its procedures. Omarska was a military camp, Your Honour, and the judicial system - and I'm referring to the wartime judicial system - had nothing to do with it. Omarska is known as a war camp, held by the Krajina Corps, I think, headed by General Talic. I think that was an error made by Mrs. Plavsic, whether intentional or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Canivell has put a question to you about your awareness, and I'd like to repeat that question in simple terms: Were you aware of killings taking place in detention camps or facilities within the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware of ill-treatment taking place in those facilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any television reports on those camps by CNN?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did it come into your mind that what you saw needed, as far as the treatment of detainees showed, that it would need some explanation as far as the treatment of those detainees are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The commission of the judiciary, headed by Slobodan Avlijas, submitted its reports to the government on several occasions, and this was a matter of discussion on the inhumane treatment of prisoners and the poor conditions in these facilities. And the reports of these commissions are held by Mr. Tieger in his file, and these were -- this was something that we discussed, I think it was in Belgrade in October last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were aware of ill-treatment in those camps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- that was the motive why we formed the commission, in order to obtain more information on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where you answered to my question, "Were you aware of ill-treatment taking place in those facilities?", your answer "no" is -- how do we have to understand that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, nobody was aware of what was going on in certain areas of Republika Srpska. When we gained information, either through the media or from Ms. Plavsic or from other people who had information on this, the government reacted, responded, and formed commissions, either on the initiative of the MUP, as we saw yesterday or the day before yesterday, that then formed mixed commissions that went on the ground, directly to these facilities, to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you form any opinion -- well, let's take again Omarska as an example, but if you'd rather prefer Manjaca, that's fine as well. Did you form any opinion as to the status of those detained in camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I learnt later on, Omarska and Manjaca were military prisons formed on the basis of the orders of the commanders of the respective territories, and they came under the exclusive jurisdiction of the army, and none of us members of the civilian government structure had any information on these matters, nor have I ever in my life been either at Omarska or at Manjaca. I was not privy to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My -- you say you had no information. Does that mean that you never formed any opinion about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having had no information, I had no views on that. When we started receiving information through the army and the police, that is, through the report of the minister of the MUP, certain commanders, and Ms. Plavsic, we took certain views, and on several occasions asked for a session of the Assembly to be called to discuss these issues, to find solutions, to establish commissions, and it seems to me that even the president of the Republic issued an order for these camps to be disbanded and to be taken out of the army's jurisdiction. My personal impression was that the response to the situation was a belated one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the work of the committee for the exchange, the state committee, would that -- the work of that committee include all types of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why were civilians exchanged rather than just released, if there was no suspicion against them and they were nevertheless held in camps or facilities, whatever you call it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that the people who were civilians, who were exchanged -- I know from firsthand knowledge that people were released to the areas where they wanted to go. As far as Kula was concerned, I had -- I have firsthand knowledge from there. Especially in the beginning of the war, I was not aware of how these exchanges took place at different, other detentions, and I don't know who the persons exchanged were, whether they were civilians, combatants, or which category they belonged to. I had no knowledge of that. It was only in the Sarajevo area that I was aware of what was going on from the month of May onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this Chamber has received evidence to the extent that persons in detention camps or in detention facilities, including civilians, were never asked where they wanted to go; they were just taken to places. Is that something you can imagine that, according to your information, that may have happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Your Honour. On the 20th of May, the second day of my term as minister, I went to the Kula facility and asked the people I found there who were leaving, and asked them where they were going. They said that they were going to Sarajevo. And with the approval of the minister of MUP, I escorted them to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My question was about evidence we received about persons in detention camps or in detention facilities, not specifically Kula. So apart from Kula, is based on the information you had at that time, is it possible that people were taken to places without being asked whether they wanted to go there, including civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you -- could you tell me what information, then, puts you in a position that you say that could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that later on I became a member of a commission that cooperated with UNPROFOR and the other commissions from the federal Sarajevo, and people talked about what had happened in some of the camps, especially the ones in Krajina, and that's when I got to know how these people were treated, what the paramilitary formations and other outsider groups and certain individuals who held power in these regions were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about a convoy passing through Pale, a large number of people, of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Sarajevo, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not from Sarajevo, but passing through Pale, brought to Pale, and then transported again from Pale, a large group of Muslim persons, including civilians, in buses.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally I have got a few questions for you on the investigations. You said the SAOs were acting almost independently. At the same time, I do understand that there was a tour around the camps which would cover the territories of the SAOs as well, in the early August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that the state authority could be exercised also on the territories of the SAOs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the central state authority gradually assumed the powers of the SAOs and centralised the government. In August, I believe, the SAOs were abolished at one of the Assembly sessions. I can't recall when exactly that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of politicians, local politicians, meeting at a central level? And when I'm talking about politicians, I'm mainly referring to the prevailing party, which was the SDS. So meeting centrally.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember when this happened? Did this happen -- let me just go through the specific month of 1992. Did this happen in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, Your Honour, but I do know that the leadership from Pale often went to different areas of Republika Srpska and scheduled meetings with the political leaderships in these respective areas. I know that they went to Bileca, Trebinje, Banja Luka, Bijeljina, Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And their local SDS politician would meet with the central leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Finally, I'd like to ask you about investigation of war crimes. Have there been bodies established to investigate the commission of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I believe this took place in a later stage of the war. I heard that these bodies were established, that there were investigations, but not in 1992, while I was in the government. I think that there was no such body at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you ever appointed to any body that would investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever appoint others on bodies which were to investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these were commissions attached to the government or the ministry, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any remembrance on when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely, but I think it must have been in August or September 1992, but I cannot recall the precise date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember whether such a commission established at that time - if it's clear enough in your memory - whether they had a task to investigate or examine all war crimes or only a certain portion of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the intention was to investigate everything that had to do with the war crimes, all the information received by the MUP and the military security, and that reports were drafted to that effect which were then forwarded to the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did there ever exist a body by the name "State Commission for Examining War Crimes Committed against Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm not privy to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you ever confronted during your interviews with a document which contains information about the existence of such a committee, of such a commission? Let me read a few lines from your interview, page 138, 139. When you were asked: "Is there any reason that the commission is expressed to be a commission inquiring only into crimes against Serbs?" And then your answer starts: "Well, the reason was that --" so you explained why this was the case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.
