utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to see the relevant portion of your interview to refresh your memory? I do not have a B/C/S version of the interview. Could either party assist me in, first of all, to provide a B/C/S version of the March 2004 interview and to locate where we find the relevant portion, which is in the English text on page 138, spilling over to 139?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We can't, Your Honour, because we've got notes all over our copies. So I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can't help with that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution usually doesn't work from the B/C/S version, I do understand. Is there any -- could you perhaps check whether there are also notes on those two specific pages? There might be notes on all pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but ... We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be read out and I could listen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it could be, but I'd rather -- of course, I've done that more or less in English, and it has been translated to you, but that doesn't seem to ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have clean -- a clean copy of those pages. We would still prefer it, if we may, if the Prosecution can spare their version, because Ms. Cmeric clearly would prefer to have it while we're working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if the Prosecution copy is readily available, but otherwise ours is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I see two persons seeking desperately and not coming up with a lot of results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we the perhaps only for --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- said, Your Honour. Apart from that preference, of course, if it's going to hold things up, here we are. I hate to see the Prosecution in desperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if you just give them in the following order to the -- to Mr. Mandic. Mr. Mandic, if you could try to find on those pages where the question is put to you whether there's any reason that the commission is expressed to be a commission inquiring only into crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does this refresh your memory as far as the existence of a commission -- is concerned with a name expressing that they would examine -- that they would inquire only into crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever a commission established to inquire into war crimes against non-Serbs or ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was, and it was attached to the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any further details, and could you tell us about the results of such a committee, or commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Minister Mico Stanisic and Assistant Minister Tomo Kovac talked of this commission, because on the ground in the areas controlled by the Serbs, there were many killings of Muslim civilians by paramilitaries and other formations, and this constituted a great difficulty, problem, for Republika Srpska. And I'm almost certain that it was the MUP of Republika Srpska that established a commission for the war crimes committed against the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the results?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with those, Your Honour. I don't know what they had done. Because this was the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor's offices, because these were acts committed by the military personnel, and the military justice system that was present in the area where the crimes committed [as interpreted] directly were the ones in charge. I don't know anything about it at the level of the government. There were, however, fully effective final decisions taken by courts for the crimes committed against the non-Serbs. These were decisions, judgements rendered by the military courts, and I know that for a fact. I think one of the judges' name is Jamina. He tried in the cases involving war crimes against the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in late 1992 that this trial took place, and I remember the discussions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have one trial on your mind or more?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there was more than one trial, Your Honour, but I know that Mr. Jamina tried such cases and that he told me personally, as this was a military secret and had to do with the military judiciary, that he had tried members of paramilitary units who had killed civilians on the territory of Republika Srpska around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo. I think his name was Dragan Jamina. He was a judge of the military court of the Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any regular military men, so not paramilitary, but any regular military men prosecuted for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us any more information about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Colovic, whom we have mentioned several times, he was the first president of the State Commission for Exchange, in the meantime was appointed judge of the supreme court, and he could tell you a lot more about this, because he was in charge of the military judiciary. And now he is the public prosecutor in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I have no further questions to you. Mr. Tieger, are there any questions that arise out of the examination of the witness by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I'm hesitant to ask you, Mr. Stewart, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We might as well go through the motions, Your Honour. Your Honour is asking me, and well my answer really is just a corollary of the more general position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I hope that you appreciate that it's my duty to ask you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I do appreciate and understand that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, this concludes your testimony in this case before the Tribunal. You have followed the discussion where the Defence has indicated that it very likely would come with a motion to be allowed to fully cross-examine you, cross-examination that has not taken place until now. In this very specific situation where, usually, once a witness is excused, he is free to discuss his testimony with anyone, under these specific circumstances, I'd like to instruct you, because there is a chance that you'll be called, or by in whatever way be cross-examined, that you not speak about your testimony with anyone, the testimony you've given until now, and whether there is -- will be any testimony still to be given is uncertain at this moment. As soon as it would be clear whether there will be any further examination, the Chamber will take care that you're informed. If no further examination will take place, the Chamber will also take care to pass a message to you so that you're not bound by these instructions any more. Mr. Mandic, these were the technicalities -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have perhaps a problem with other cases or?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have some concern about the order. If I may be given just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that there may be a certain interest at the Prosecution side to have further discussions with Mr. Mandic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly that's part of it, and there's -- I think other concerns arise as well that are worth addressing, and I'd like a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, I first of all would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and to have answered all questions put to you. It might be that the instructions I just gave to you will be altered, will be changed, because it creates some problems for the Prosecution. You'll be properly informed about it if the instructions undergo any changes. I'll take care that at least you receive the changed instructions in such a way, preferably in writing, that there can be no misunderstanding as to what instructions you're bound by. Mr. Tomic, I'd like to ask you as well for your presence. Mr. Tieger, I take it that we can deal with the matter in the absence of the witness, in view of what I've just said, that he'll be informed about --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Mandic and Mr. Tomic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we deal with the matter right away. Mr. Tieger, do you think that it can be done in open session or would there be any reason to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think private session is probably preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Preferable, Your Honour, but may we know the reasons, which must be very specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I can imagine that sometimes reasons should be given in private session to start with and then we'll decide whether we remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. With respect, Your Honour, yes, then, but as soon as we go into private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of December 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
